items.title: Speech by SJ at plenary session of 16th China-ASEAN Prosecutors-General Conference in Brunei (English only)
items.description: Following is the speech by the Secretary for Justice, Mr Paul Lam, SC, at the plenary session of the 16th China-ASEAN Prosecutors-General Conference in Brunei today (October 22): Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, Children today grow up in an interconnected digital world that offers unprecedented opportunities for education and development. But at the same time, modern technology exposes them to grave and fast-evolving risks - from violent or pornographic content on social media platforms, to online grooming, non-consensual sharing of intimate images, deepfake manipulation, cyberbullying, coercion and fraud. The stark reality is that digital harm to children knows no borders. For example, an intimate image of a child, once created or uploaded, can be copied, disseminated and recirculated repeatedly and instantaneously across different jurisdictions. A child may have to live with the fear that such material will resurface at any time, transforming a single act of abuse into a cycle of victimisation. Against this backdrop, protecting children in the digital age is an urgent, shared regional and international responsibility which demands synchronised legal and institutional responses. Hong Kong's existing legal framework In this respect, Hong Kong maintains a solid legal framework to protect children from online sexual exploitation and other forms of cyber-enabled crime. To begin with, the Prevention of Child Pornography Ordinance criminalises a broad range of conduct involving child pornography, including printing, producing, copying, importing, exporting, publishing, and possessing child pornography, with maximum penalties ranging from three to eight years' imprisonment upon conviction. The Ordinance includes express provisions for the forfeiture of any child pornography, as well as any machinery or apparatus used to commit the relevant offences. Importantly, the statutory definition of "child pornography" under the Ordinance encompasses any "computer-generated image or other visual depiction" - irrespective of whether it is generated by electronic or other means, whether it depicts a real person, or whether it has been "modified". The Ordinance thus extends beyond traditional physical media to capture synthetic, computer-generated, or altered materials. This statutory definition is vital in ensuring that our legal framework remains future-proofed against rapid technological change. Another milestone in Hong Kong's legislative framework is the enactment of the comprehensive voyeurism and non-consensual intimate image regime under Part XIIAA of the Crimes Ordinance in 2021. Voyeurism covers acts of observing or recording, with or without equipment, another person's intimate part or doing an intimate act without consent for the purpose of obtaining sexual gratification or causing humiliation, distress, or alarm. This law also criminalises acts of non-consensual recording, publication and threatened publication of intimate images, carrying maximum penalties up to five years' imprisonment. "Intimate image" under the Ordinance includes an image that has been altered to appear to show an intimate part or an individual doing an intimate act, providing a clear legal basis to tackle digital editing and manipulation - tactics increasingly used for online extortion and sexual exploitation. Significantly, the legislation provides that a child under 16 is legally incapable of giving consent. This provides vital protection for young people vulnerable to online image exploitation. Furthermore, the statutory framework empowers our courts to issue a disposal order requiring any person, whether in Hong Kong and elsewhere, to take reasonable steps to remove, delete, or destroy such images, at any stage during criminal proceedings, and its validity remains unaffected even if the prosecution is subsequently discontinued or the defendant is acquitted. Importantly, the court can order the service of such disposal order on a person or entity out of jurisdiction. This extra-territorial mechanism applies to online platforms and social media providers operating outside Hong Kong, ensuring that our laws do not merely punish offenders but actively disrupt the cycle of victimisation at its source. The above statutes are examples of Hong Kong's legislation tailored specifically to child protection. But it must be borne in mind that many traditional criminal offences are "technologically neutral" - meaning that the law applies with equal force regardless of whether the offence is committed physically or via digital means. For instance, cyberbullying or online extortion may be prosecuted under offences such as criminal intimidation, carrying a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment, or blackmail with a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. In a Court of Appeal case decided back in 2018, the defendant who secretly recorded intimate videos of his partner and threatened their online dissemination to her colleagues and friends was convicted for, among other things, the offence of criminal intimidation. The Court laid down key sentencing principles for secret filming - specifically recognising the grave risk of rapid, indefinite online spread. Child protection as a shared responsibility Having said all these, we recognise that maintaining existing a legal framework alone is not enough. As the Court of Appeal highlighted in the recent case decided earlier this year, young and inexperienced users are increasingly vulnerable to being lured into harm through online dating and networking platforms. In that case, a 16-year-old girl was lured via a dating app by a 41-year-old man posing as a 27 year old, leading to sexual abuse and rape. The Court of Appeal remarked that owners and operators of social media, dating applications, and other online platforms cannot treat criminal conduct on their services as a matter solely for law enforcement. Rather, platform providers play a pivotal role in shaping a safe online environment. This case serves as an important reminder that child protection in the digital age is a shared responsibility that cannot rely solely on criminal prosecution. Safeguarding children from modern virtual risks requires a co-ordinated strategy combining effective legislation, rigorous law enforcement, industry accountability, early intervention, and public education. Hong Kong's responses to emerging risks In response to the growing need to protect children amidst rapid technological change, Hong Kong has advanced a series of key initiatives for better protection of children. As a broader strategic background, Hong Kong published its First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development (First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2026-2030)) on September 16, 2026, in alignment with the National 15th Five-Year Plan. The Plan sets down long-term strategic directives to, among other key areas, fortify security governance, combat newly emerged cybercrimes through deeper cross-boundary law enforcement collaboration, and enhance child welfare and abuse reporting mechanisms. First, the Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) has announced in the Policy Address 2026 that a dedicated task force on minors' use of social media will be established under the Inter-Departmental Working Group to Review Legislation to Support Wider Application of AI spearheaded by the Department of Justice. The task force will review the risks associated with the use of social media by minors, and assess the need for more targeted legislative and administrative solutions. In considering the way forward, the Government will study international regulatory models and explore measures suitable for Hong Kong, particularly regarding the responsibilities of Internet service providers. For instance: (1) whether the platforms should be required to systematically identify risk of criminal conduct on their services and implement effective user warnings; (2) whether heightened protective measures and age-related safeguards should be mandated for minor users; (3) whether the platforms should maintain simple, accessible reporting mechanisms for suspicious or abusive behaviour that trigger transparent, effective responses, including timely co-operation with law enforcement agencies. The purpose of this initiative is not to isolate children from technology, nor to restrict their digital participation and fundamental rights. Rather, it is to ensure that children will not be exposed to risks and can engage with the online world safely, with appropriate safeguards against misinformation, harmful materials, or even illegal content. Of course, legislative intervention is one among many tools. We need hard law on the one hand and soft mechanisms - such as industry guidelines, codes of conduct, and public education - on the other to drive proactive compliance. These tools are not mutually exclusive; they should operate in parallel. To this end, as also announced in the Policy Address 2026, the Education Bureau of the Hong Kong SAR will support schools in guiding students to use AI tools prudently, equipping them with the digital literacy and values needed to navigate online risks. Second, also under the strategic directions of the Five-Year Plan and the Policy Address 2026, the Cybercrime Sub-committee of the Law Reform Commission is conducting an in-depth review of our legal framework, focusing specifically on AI-enabled crimes, including those targeting children. Having published its first report recommending bespoke cybercrime legislation, the Sub-committee's ongoing work centres on formulating robust statutory measures to tackle the illicit production of synthetic pornographic images, online fraud, and deepfake exploitation directed at minors. Third, the Hong Kong SAR Government will introduce an amendment bill to comprehensively reform our sexual offence regime. This includes eight new bespoke child sexual offences, such as grooming, causing a child to view sexual images, and engaging in sexual communication with a child. These targeted proposals address modern online harms, from cyberflashing, online sexual exploitation, to digital sex trafficking. Fourth, the Department of Justice has established a dedicated task force on vulnerable witnesses and child protection. Bringing together its Prosecutions Division, the Hong Kong Police Force, and the Social Welfare Department, this specialised task force fosters seamless multi-agency collaboration - facilitating early prosecutor intervention, expedited legal advice, and tailored court safeguards to minimise trauma for child victims throughout the judicial process. Under this joint framework, this task force has issued around 900 pieces of advice the since its inception in 2022. Fifth, given the transnational nature of online child sexual exploitation, the Hong Kong Police Force has actively deepened international co-operation. In 2025, the Force joined the International Child Sexual Exploitation database of the INTERPOL (International Criminal Police Organization), an intelligence and investigative platform through which specialised investigators utilise advanced algorithms and intelligence sharing across more than 70 jurisdictions to identify victims and offenders. In addition, the Police Force regularly participates in joint multi-jurisdictional operations. Notably, from March to April this year, Hong Kong joined law enforcement agencies from Brunei, Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea, and Thailand in a co-ordinated operation against child pornography, resulting in 326 arrests and the seizure of various mobile devices containing child pornographic materials. The need for international co-operation As I mentioned at the outset, cybercrimes targeted at children know no jurisdictional limits. Cross-border co-operation is indispensable. In this regard, I wish to highlight four essential areas for our joint collaborative efforts in child protection in the modern technological era. First, keeping our legal frameworks abreast of technological change requires sharing of knowledge and experience. As cyber threats rapidly evolve, no single jurisdiction has all the answers. By sharing regulatory approaches and law drafting experiences, we can refine and update our existing laws. Wherever appropriate, legislation should be designed with extra-territorial application. This is essential to enable effective investigation and prosecution when offenders operate in one country, target children in another, and disseminate abusive material across platforms hosted in a third. Secondly, effective mutual legal assistance arrangements and adaptable evidence rules are essential for prosecuting transnational crimes where overseas evidence and child witnesses are involved. In Hong Kong, under Part IIIA of the Criminal Procedure Ordinance, child witnesses who may not be able to endure the pressure of testifying in a traditional courtroom are permitted to give evidence via a live video-link or through pre-recorded interviews. Further, under Part VIIIA of the Evidence Ordinance, our courts may issue letters of request to foreign authorities to obtain evidence out of the jurisdiction, which is a very useful tool to obtain evidence in transboundary crimes. In addition, relaxing the exceptions to the criminal hearsay rule under the common law is necessary to enable that the admissibility of foreign digital logs, records, and out-of-court statements in criminal proceedings. In this regard, Hong Kong is introducing a major reform of the hearsay rule in criminal and surrender proceedings under the Evidence (Amendment) Bill 2026 which was gazetted on June 12, 2026. Thirdly, priority should be given to deepening co-operation between law enforcement agencies worldwide. As the Hong Kong experience shows, co-ordinated action can produce fruitful and meaningful results. Our respective law enforcement agencies should establish clear and accessible communication channels with each other so as to facilitate the timely exchange of information and intelligence. Information shared promptly may enable authorities to identify children at immediate risk, locate offenders, or prevent the circulation of harmful material. By maintaining regular liaison at both the strategic and operational levels, we can significantly improve our ability to identify offenders of cross-border cybercrime and child exploitation early, and take prompt intervention action to disrupt cybercrime networks. Lastly, we should not lose sight of the importance of continuous training and professional development of officers involved in the protection of children against transnational cybercrime. Specialist training is critical to protecting children in the digital age. Law enforcement agencies and other professionals working in this area must be well equipped to recognise the indicators of online grooming, AI-facilitated exploitation, and child abuse activities in various forms and manifestations. To this extent, regular international conferences and symposiums, meetings and working groups, as well as training courses, workshops, and seminars have an important role to play in cultivating our professional expertise. If cybercriminals can adapt and learn quickly from one another, we must be able to do better. Conclusion Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. It is often said that children are the future of the world. As prosecutors and ministers of justice representing our communities, it is incumbent upon us to ensure that children in this day and age can grow, learn, and explore in the digital world without being exposed to exploitation, abuse, or manipulation. That can only be done if governments join hands to take effective measures locally, regionally, and globally, to strengthen co-operation at all levels and among all relevant agencies. As I have said before, "alone we can do so little, together we can do so much". On behalf of the Hong Kong SAR, I can say loud and clear that all branches of our Government will continue to promote international co-operation to better the protection for children amidst the digital age in all ways possible. On this note, may I once conclude by congratulating the Attorney General's Chambers of Brunei Darussalam for holding this important and successful conference, and expressing our utmost gratitude to your warm hospitality. My gratitude also goes to all the distinguished speakers for sharing their invaluable insights and experience. Thank you very much.

items.title: Government Laboratory signs amended Memorandum of Understanding on Cooperation with National Institute of Metrology, China (with photos)
items.description: The Government Laboratory (GL) of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region and the National Institute of Metrology, China (NIM) today (October 22) signed an amended Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on Cooperation in Beijing, with the aim of further deepening exchanges and co-operation between the two parties in the field of metrology, and enhancing their capabilities and expertise in chemistry and related measurement disciplines. NIM is the nation's highest research facility of measurement science, and a national statutory authority in the field of metrology. The GL, as the designated institute representing Hong Kong, China in the field of chemical metrology, has been disseminating traceability of chemical measurements to local laboratories, thereby enhancing the reliability and accuracy of chemical testing results within the testing sector. ​ The MOU on Cooperation was signed by the Government Chemist, Dr Cheung Tsz-chun, and the Director General of NIM, Dr Li Wentao. According to the MOU on Cooperation, both sides will continue to deepen exchanges in the fields of chemistry and related metrology disciplines, and foster a long-term partnership. Dr Cheung said, "As the country is fully implementing the 15th Five-Year Plan, metrology, as a vital foundation for scientific and technological innovation and high-quality development, faces higher expectations and greater opportunities. Through this MOU on Cooperation, the GL looks forward to strengthening communication, deepening personnel exchanges and capability building, and jointly enhancing metrological capabilities to support and serve the high-quality development of the country and the region." The GL delegation yesterday (October 21) and today also engaged in detailed exchanges with NIM scientific experts, visited scientific facilities at NIM's Changping Campus and Hepingli Campus, and gained an understanding of the production process and approval procedures for Reference Materials.

items.title: Unemployment and underemployment statistics for July - September 2026
items.description: According to the latest labour force statistics (i.e. provisional figures for July - September 2026) released today (October 22) by the Census and Statistics Department (C&SD), the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate increased from 3.8% in June - August 2026 to 3.9% in July - September 2026. The underemployment rate also increased from 1.9% in June - August 2026 to 2.0% in July - September 2026. Comparing July - September 2026 with June - August 2026, movements in the unemployment rate (not seasonally adjusted) in different industry sectors varied, with more distinct increases observed in the social work activities sector, and warehousing and support activities for transportation sector. As to the underemployment rate, increases were mainly seen in the food and beverage service activities sector and retail sector. Total employment increased by around 3 000 from 3 652 000 in June - August 2026 to 3 655 000 in July - September 2026. Over the same period, the labour force also increased by around 4 100 from 3 805 900 to 3 810 000. The number of unemployed persons (not seasonally adjusted) increased by around 1 100 from 153 900 in June - August 2026 to 155 000 in July - September 2026. Over the same period, the number of underemployed persons also increased by around 2 900 from 72 100 to 75 000. Commentary Commenting on the latest unemployment figures, the Secretary for Labour and Welfare, Mr Chris Sun, said, "The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate edged up by 0.1 percentage point over the preceding three-month period to 3.9% in July - September 2026. The underemployment rate also rose slightly by 0.1 percentage point to 2.0%. Over the same period, both the labour force and total employment increased further amid the continued influx of fresh graduates and school leavers into the labour market." Looking ahead, Mr Sun said, "The sustained expansion of the local economy, improving business sentiment and continued growth in visitor arrivals are expected to underpin the overall employment situation, particularly in the consumption- and tourism-related sectors. Meanwhile, the Government will continue to closely monitor the potential impacts of external uncertainties on corporate hiring sentiments and provide job-seekers with appropriate support." Further information The unemployment and underemployment statistics were compiled from the findings of the continuous General Household Survey. In the survey, the definitions used in measuring unemployment and underemployment follow closely those recommended by the International Labour Organization. The employed population covers all employers, self-employed persons, employees (including full-time, part-time, casual workers, etc.) and unpaid family workers. Unemployed persons by industry (or occupation) are classified according to their previous industry (or occupation). The survey for July - September 2026 covered a sample of some 25 000 households or 65 000 persons, selected in accordance with a scientifically designed sampling scheme to represent the population of Hong Kong. Labour force statistics compiled from this sample represented the situation in the moving three-month period of July to September 2026. Data on labour force characteristics were obtained from the survey by interviewing each member aged 15 or over in the sampled households. Statistical tables on the latest labour force statistics can be downloaded at the website of the C&SD ( www.censtatd.gov.hk/en/scode200.html ). More detailed analysis of the labour force characteristics is given in the "Quarterly Report on General Household Survey" which is published four times a year. The latest issue of the report contains statistics for the quarter April - June 2026 while the next issue covering the quarter July - September 2026 will be available by end November 2026. Users can also browse and download this publication at the website of the C&SD ( www.censtatd.gov.hk/en/EIndexbySubject.html?pcode=B1050001&scode=200 ). For enquiries about labour force statistics, please contact the General Household Survey Section (3) of the C&SD (Tel: 2887 5508 or email: ghs@censtatd.gov.hk ).

items.title: Consumer Price Indices for September 2026
items.description: The Census and Statistics Department (C&SD) released today (October 22) the Consumer Price Index (CPI) figures for September 2026. According to the Composite CPI, overall consumer prices rose by 1.9% in September 2026 over the same month a year earlier, larger than the corresponding increase (1.7%) in August 2026. Netting out the effects of all Government's one-off relief measures, the year-on-year rate of increase in the Composite CPI (i.e. the underlying inflation rate) in September 2026 was 2.1%, also larger than that in August 2026 (1.9%). The larger increase in September 2026 was mainly due to the accelerated increases in inbound and outbound transport fares and the charges for package holidays. On a seasonally adjusted basis, the average monthly rate of increase in the Composite CPI for the 3-month period ending September 2026 was 0.2%, the same as that for the 3-month period ending August 2026. Netting out the effects of all Government's one-off relief measures, the corresponding rates of increase were both 0.2%. Analysed by sub-index, the year-on-year rates of increase in the CPI(A), CPI(B) and CPI(C) were 1.4%, 2.0% and 2.3% respectively in September 2026, as compared to 1.2%, 1.8% and 1.9% respectively in August 2026. Netting out the effects of all Government's one-off relief measures, the year-on-year rates of increase in the CPI(A), CPI(B) and CPI(C) were 1.7%, 2.2% and 2.4% respectively in September 2026, as compared to 1.6%, 2.0% and 2.0% respectively in August 2026. On a seasonally adjusted basis, for the 3-month period ending September 2026, the average monthly rates of increase in the CPI(A), CPI(B) and CPI(C) were all 0.2%. The corresponding rates of increase for the 3-month period ending August 2026 were 0.2%, 0.1% and 0.1% respectively. Netting out the effects of all Government's one-off relief measures, the average monthly rates of increase in the seasonally adjusted CPI(A), CPI(B) and CPI(C) for the 3-month period ending September 2026 were 0.1%, 0.2% and 0.2% respectively, and the corresponding rates of increase for the 3-month period ending August 2026 were 0.2%, 0.1% and 0.1% respectively. Amongst the various components of the Composite CPI, year-on-year increases in prices were recorded in September 2026 for electricity, gas and water (12.9%), miscellaneous services (5.3%), transport (5.2%), miscellaneous goods (2.1%), durable goods (1.1%), meals out and takeaway food (1.0%), clothing and footwear (0.3%), and housing (0.2%). On the other hand, year-on-year decreases in the components of the Composite CPI were recorded in September 2026 for alcoholic drinks and tobacco (-0.4%), and basic food (-0.2%). Taking the first 9 months of 2026 together, the Composite CPI rose by 1.7% over the same period a year earlier. The respective increases in the CPI(A), CPI(B) and CPI(C) were 1.5%, 1.8% and 1.9% respectively. The corresponding increases after netting out the effects of all Government's one-off relief measures were 1.7%, 1.4%, 1.8% and 1.9% respectively. In the third quarter of 2026, the Composite CPI rose by 1.7% over the same period a year earlier, while the CPI(A), CPI(B) and CPI(C) rose by 1.3%, 1.9% and 2.1% respectively. The corresponding increases after netting out the effects of all Government's one-off relief measures were 2.0%, 1.7%, 2.1% and 2.2% respectively. For the 12 months ending September 2026, the Composite CPI on average rose by 1.6% over the same period a year earlier. The respective increases in the CPI(A), CPI(B) and CPI(C) were 1.5%, 1.7% and 1.7% respectively. The corresponding increases after netting out the effects of all Government's one-off relief measures were 1.6%, 1.3%, 1.6% and 1.7% respectively. Commentary A Government spokesman said that the underlying Composite CPI rose by 2.1% in September over a year earlier, up from 1.9% in the preceding month, largely driven by faster price increases in fuel-related items. Yet, price increases of other components were largely modest, thus keeping overall inflation moderate. Looking ahead, consumer price inflation will remain under upward pressure, as persistently elevated international oil prices feed through to fuel-related components amid ongoing geopolitical tension in the Middle East. Yet, as price pressures on other fronts are expected to remain largely contained, overall inflation should stay moderate. items.title: Hong Kong Customs detects four sea smuggling cases and seizes suspected illicit cigarettes worth about $230 million (with photos)
items.description: ​Hong Kong Customs detected four sea smuggling cases via intelligence exchanges and analysis. More than 51 million suspected illicit cigarettes with a total estimated market value of about $230 million and a duty potential of about $170 million were seized. Through intelligence exchanges with law enforcement agencies in the region and further intelligence analysis, Customs from August to September selected and examined five 40-foot seaborne containers arriving in Hong Kong from the South Asian region and declared as carrying clothes, lighting equipment, electronic parts and hydraulic components, at the Kwai Chung Customhouse Cargo Examination Compound. Large quantities of illicit cigarettes were seized. Preliminary investigation revealed that the batch of illicit cigarettes was destined for other countries or regions but was all intercepted by Hong Kong Customs while in transit. The investigation is still ongoing. The likelihood of arrests is not ruled out. The cases displayed Customs' enforcement effectiveness in intercepting cross-border illicit cigarettes at the source through co-operation with law enforcement agencies in the region. The department will continue to foster collaboration and strengthen intelligence exchanges between regional partners in law enforcement, and vigorously combat cross-border illicit cigarette activities. Customs will continue its risk assessment and intelligence analysis, and step up enforcement actions to combat smuggling of illicit cigarettes. Customs stresses that smuggling is a serious offence. Under the Import and Export Ordinance (Cap. 60), any person found guilty of importing or exporting unmanifested cargo is liable to a maximum fine of $2 million and imprisonment for seven years. Moreover, under the Dutiable Commodities Ordinance (Cap. 109), any person who deals with, possesses, sells or buys illicit cigarettes commits an offence. The maximum penalty upon conviction is a fine of $2 million and imprisonment for seven years. Members of the public may report any suspected illicit cigarette activities to Customs' 24-hour hotline 182 8080 or its dedicated crime-reporting email account ( crimereport@customs.gov.hk ) or online form ( eform.cefs.gov.hk/form/ced002 ).

items.title: Oilex and HNS exercises test marine pollution responses (with photos)
items.description: The annual marine pollution joint response exercises, codenamed "Oilex 2026" and "Maritime Hazardous and Noxious Substances (HNS) 2026", were conducted by various government departments this morning (October 22) in the waters off Mo Tat Wan of Lamma Island to test their marine pollution responses in the event of a spillage of oil and HNS in Hong Kong waters. In the test scenario, an oil tanker collided with a container vessel, resulting in fuel oil spilling from the oil tanker, and five containers loaded with Maleic anhydride falling overboard. Subsequently, an oil spill response team arrived on the scene and cleaned up the spilled oil on the sea surface. The Fire Services Department (FSD) and other response groups were also tasked at the scene to contain and handle the probable spilled Maleic anhydride as necessary to prevent threats to the nearby environment and facilities. During the exercises, various participating parties carried out a series of simulated response actions. After the simulated oil spill, the oil tanker anchored in the waters off Mo Tat Wan, while a salvage team transferred the fuel oil from the damaged tank and patched the leak to stop further oil spillage at the source. Moreover, an oil pollution combat team deployed floating barrier booms to encircle the oil tanker and set up barrier booms in the vicinity to prevent the spill from spreading. The exercise also simulated the spraying of oil dispersant with water from pollution control vessels and a Government Flying Service (GFS) helicopter onto oil on the sea surface, as well as the use of oil skimmers and other equipment. Simultaneously, a shoreline cleaning team conducted a shoreline oil clean-up drill at the non-gazetted beach of Mo Tat Wan. In combating the simulated HNS spill, the response groups lifted the damaged containers out from the sea to stop the pollution at the source. The joint response exercises were co-ordinated by the Marine Department and the Environmental Protection Department. The participating government departments and organisations included the FSD, the GFS, the Hong Kong Police Force, the Government Laboratory and the Civil Aid Service, as well as several oil companies and a pollution control company jointly formed by them. The response exercises not only provided hands-on experience for response members but also helped relevant parties to adopt an effective emergency response strategy for preventing pollution according to the properties and extents of spilled substances.

items.title: Speech by FS at OASES Enterprises Signing Ceremony (English only) (with photos/video)
items.description: Following is the speech by the Financial Secretary, Mr Paul Chan, at the OASES Enterprises Signing Ceremony today (October 22): Peter (Director-General of the Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises (OASES), Mr Peter Yan), government colleagues, strategic enterprise partners, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, Good afternoon. A very warm welcome to our 18 new strategic enterprise partners. Your businesses cover a remarkably wide range of sectors, from advanced manufacturing and new energy to artificial intelligence, life and health technology, fintech, and cultural and creative technology. Several of you have market capitalisation or valuation exceeding HK$100 billion. And all of you bring capabilities that will help shape the next stage of Hong Kong's development. Today, half of our new partners come from the Chinese Mainland, while the other half from various parts of the world. That diversity speaks to Hong Kong's role: a place where businesses, talent and ideas from around the world come together to prosper. Together, with enterprises in earlier batches, the 142 strategic enterprises are expected to bring in some HK$84 billion of investment and create about 27,000 jobs. We appreciate your contributions, and look forward to working with you to turn them into lasting commercial success and real benefits for the community. Indeed, the growth of our strategic enterprises has been impressive. Consider the first six batches of enterprises. Their total investment has exceeded expectations by 30 per cent, while the jobs created by 34 per cent. Altogether, they have taken up more than 2.8 million square feet of commercial and industrial space. Yet these figures tell only part of the story. What matters is the difference these enterprises can make in driving our innovation and technology sector forward, providing new impetus to our economy and employment, as well as solutions that make people live better. For example, one of the strategic enterprises in this batch has developed real-time AI-empowered risk scores to predict patient deterioration in general wards and intensive care units, allowing medical intervention to come much earlier. Another strategic enterprise will deploy its AI+Smart vehicle technologies and Internet of Vehicles applications in Hong Kong to accelerate the wider adoption of EVs (electric vehicles), while using the city as a testing ground to advance green and smart mobility in the region. This is the kind of impact we would like to see. And we are determined to create the conditions for more impact, by connecting finance, research, talent and industry more effectively, and by making it easier for enterprises to scale up their operations as well as products and services. As we take forward Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan, innovation and technology is a key priority within our "four centres and one hub" development framework. We will put our financial strengths to work for technological innovation, helping enterprises secure capital as they develop, commercialise and expand. That is what we mean by "Finance+": finance empowering innovation and the real economy. The Northern Metropolis will provide the space for realising that ambition. We are developing three university towns there to bring education, research, talent development and industry closer together. This will strengthen collaboration and accelerate the journey from laboratory discoveries to market-ready solutions. We are also strengthening these links across the Greater Bay Area. Through the Hetao Co-operation Zone, we are making it easier for people, goods, capital, data and samples to flow across the boundary. Take biomedicine as an example. Smoother cross-boundary flows of research data and biological samples will support research and development. And the Mainland and Hong Kong authorities are stepping up collaboration on clinical trials and drug approvals. These efforts will help companies bring new treatments to patients more quickly, both on the Mainland and in the international markets. No wonder many global pharmaceutical firms are choosing Hong Kong as their R&D (research and development) hub and regional base. Ladies and gentlemen, our finance and innovation ecosystem is open to the region, and open to the world. Openness is at the heart of who we are. We thrive on international connectivity and the free flow of goods, capital, information and, above all, talent. With each new strategic enterprise, this ecosystem grows stronger. High-quality enterprises attract talented people, who bring fresh ideas and draw more businesses to Hong Kong. This virtuous cycle creates more opportunities for businesses and innovators. To our new partners, our invitation is simple: build your business here. Bring your research, nurture your talent, and use Hong Kong as a springboard to take your innovations further. Your next breakthrough may well begin here in Hong Kong, with an impact that reaches far beyond our shores. Let us work together to turn that promise into greater success, for your business and for Hong Kong. Thank you very much.

items.title: Inspection of aquatic products imported from Japan
items.description: In response to the Japanese Government's plan to discharge nuclear-contaminated water at the Fukushima Nuclear Power Station, the Director of Food and Environmental Hygiene issued a Food Safety Order which prohibits all aquatic products, sea salt and seaweeds originating from the 10 metropolis/prefectures, namely Tokyo, Fukushima, Ibaraki, Miyagi, Chiba, Gunma, Tochigi, Niigata, Nagano and Saitama, from being imported into and supplied in Hong Kong. For other Japanese aquatic products, sea salt and seaweeds that are not prohibited from being imported into Hong Kong, the Centre for Food Safety (CFS) of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department is conducting comprehensive radiological tests to verify that the radiation levels of these products do not exceed the guideline levels before they are allowed to be supplied in the market. From noon on October 21 to noon today (October 22), the CFS conducted tests on the radiological levels of 116 food samples imported from Japan, which were of the "aquatic and related products, seaweeds and sea salt" category. No sample was found to have exceeded the safety limit. Details can be found on the CFS's thematic website titled "Control Measures on Foods Imported from Japan" ( www.cfs.gov.hk/english/programme/programme_rafs/programme_rafs_fc_01_30_Nuclear_Event_and_Food_Safety.html ). In parallel, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) has also tested 50 samples of local catch for radiological levels. All the samples passed the tests. Details can be found on the AFCD's website ( www.afcd.gov.hk/english/fisheries/Radiological_testing/Radiological_Test.html ). The Hong Kong Observatory (HKO) has also enhanced the environmental monitoring of the local waters. No anomaly has been detected so far. For details, please refer to the HKO's website ( www.hko.gov.hk/en/radiation/monitoring/seawater.html ). From August 24, 2023, to noon today, the CFS and the AFCD have conducted tests on the radiological levels of 269 461 samples of food imported from Japan (including 167 721 samples of aquatic and related products, seaweeds and sea salt) and 57 410 samples of local catch respectively. All the samples passed the tests.

items.title: Incoming passenger convicted and jailed for possession of duty-not-paid cigarettes (with photos)
items.description: An incoming male passenger was sentenced to three months' imprisonment with a fine of $1,000 by the Fanling Magistrates' Courts today (October 22) for possessing duty-not-paid cigarettes and failing to declare them to Customs officers, in contravention of the Dutiable Commodities Ordinance (DCO). Customs officers intercepted the incoming 84-year-old local male passenger at the Heung Yuen Wai Boundary Control Point on September 22 and seized 801 duty-not-paid cigarettes from him. The estimated market value of the seized cigarettes was about $3,600, and the duty potential was about $2,600. The passenger was subsequently arrested. Customs welcomes the sentence. The custodial sentence has imposed a considerable deterrent effect and reflects the seriousness of the offences. Members of the public should not defy the law. Customs reminds members of the public that under the DCO, cigarettes are dutiable goods to which the DCO applies. Any person who imports, deals with, possesses, sells or buys illicit cigarettes commits an offence. The maximum penalty upon conviction is a fine of $2 million and imprisonment for seven years. items.title: CE receives report of Independent Committee in relation to fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po (with photo)
items.description: The Chief Executive, Mr John Lee, today (October 22) received the report of the Independent Committee in relation to the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po. The Chief Executive thanked the Chairman of the Independent Committee, Mr Justice David Lok, and members Mr Chan Kin-por and Dr Rex Auyeung for their efforts. Through holding evidential hearings and other means, the Independent Committee heard and considered a large amount of evidence and materials provided by witnesses, experts, organisations and so on. It has, after in-depth analysis and study, compiled a detailed report in accordance with its terms of reference, providing a comprehensive review and recommendations on the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po and on large-scale building maintenance and renovation works. The Chief Executive said, "The Government will make comprehensive reforms in areas including the supervision of building maintenance works, building management and regulation for fire service installations. The 2026 Policy Address published in September has launched various priority reform initiatives, while the Government has already taken steps to prepare for comprehensive reforms. We will carefully study the Committee's report, actively follow up on its recommendations, and shortly announce the plans for the comprehensive reforms and pursuing accountability." The Government will publish the Committee's report. As various individuals implicated in the Wang Fuk Court fire have been charged with different criminal offences, it is incumbent upon the Government to identify and consider how best to handle those parts of the report that may be involved in the criminal trials, so as not to prejudice the court proceedings. The Government will seek legal advice on the appropriate way to publish the report at the earliest possible juncture. The Chief Executive announced the establishment of the Committee on December 12, 2025, to review the causes and related issues of the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, to make recommendations to prevent similar incidents from occurring again, and to submit a report on the matter.

items.title: Independent Committee in relation to fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po submits report to Chief Executive
items.description: The following is issued on behalf of the Independent Committee in relation to the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po: The Independent Committee in relation to the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po (the Committee) has completed its inquiry work and submitted its report to the Chief Executive today (October 22). The Chief Executive announced on December 12, 2025 the establishment of the Committee to review the causes of the fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po and related issues, and to make recommendations to prevent similar incidents from occurring again. The Committee formally commenced its work on December 19, 2025. It held a total of 30 days of evidential hearings to hear oral evidence from 80 factual and expert witnesses, and submissions from the legal representatives of the involved parties. The Committee also ascertained the relevant facts through written statements submitted by different individuals and organisations, and evidence submitted in other forms. The Committee eventually obtained more than 1 million files, with the data size exceeding 2 terabytes. With the evidence and materials received as the factual framework, the Committee has completed its inquiry work on the matters set out in its terms of reference, and prepared the report accordingly.

items.title: Applications for vacant fixed hawker pitches to close next Monday
items.description: The Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD) is reallocating a total of 321 vacant fixed hawker pitches and issuing new licences. Persons who are interested in joining the hawking trade and meet the eligibility criteria may complete and submit their applications via the FEHD website ( www.fehd.gov.hk ) by 5pm on Monday (October 26). The pitches are located in Eastern District (four pitches), Central and Western District (seven pitches), Wan Chai District (26 pitches), Yau Tsim District (110 pitches), Mong Kok District (101 pitches), Sham Shui Po District (28 pitches), Kowloon City District (five pitches) and Tsuen Wan District (40 pitches). A spokesman for the FEHD said today (October 22), "Each applicant is allowed to submit one application only, and an application number will be given to individual applicants in each category, namely holders of the Fixed-Pitch (Newspaper) Hawker Licence, holders of the Itinerant Hawker Licence (Other Classes/Newspaper), eligible registered assistants meeting the application requirements, and members of the public satisfying certain basic criteria. The pitch selection priority order of eligible applicants will be generated in a fair and impartial manner by way of open computer random sequencing and manual ballot." Upon completion of the ballot, eligible applicants will receive written notification of their pitch selection priority numbers, or they can check the results on the FEHD website the following day. The FEHD will then issue letters in batches according to the pitch selection priority numbers to invite successful applicants for pitch selection and completion of the formalities for the issuance of a new licence. The spokesman added, "Except for applicants under the categories of licensed fixed-pitch newspaper hawkers or licensed itinerant hawkers, the hawker licence operation period of a newly issued hawker licence is seven years and the licence will not be renewed upon expiry. Applicants shall also design and construct the stall at their own expense in accordance with the specifications previously approved by the FEHD, and may commence business only after the stall is confirmed to be in compliance with the specifications." Members of the public can visit the FEHD website for details on the allocation of vacant fixed hawker pitches, methods of submitting applications, and stall construction requirements.

items.title: SCST congratulates Vivian Lau, Yeung Hiu-lam, Leung Yuk-wing, Cheung Yuen, Ng Cheuk-yan, John Loung, Yu Chui-yee, Tong Nga-ting and Hung Wing-long on winning medals in Asian Para Games
items.description: The Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism, Miss Rosanna Law, today (October 21) extended her congratulations to boccia athlete Vivian Lau on winning a gold medal in Women's Individual-BC4 at the 5th Asian Para Games, bringing the Hong Kong, China delegation its first gold medal of the Games. John Loung remained resilient in the bronze medal match and overhauled his opponent in the final end to claim the bronze medal. In swimming, Ng Cheuk-yan broke her personal record and won another silver medal for the swimming team, while Hung Wing-long also performed to his best to win the bronze medal. In fencing, Yu Chui-yee and Tong Nga-ting fought through a series of tight matches to claim two bronze medals for the fencing team. items.title: HKSAR Government's response to World Justice Project Rule of Law Index 2026
items.description: ​The World Justice Project released the Rule of Law Index 2026 today (October 21). Hong Kong's overall ranking remains high and unchanged, ranking 6th in East Asia and the Pacific, and 24th out of 143 countries and jurisdictions globally. Hong Kong's scores in most of the aspects are similar to those of last year, and its overall ranking continues to be ahead of some western countries which often unreasonably criticise the rule of law and human rights situation of Hong Kong. Hong Kong continues to maintain its position within the top 10 globally in respect of "Absence of Corruption" and "Order and Security", with the global ranking in relation to "Order and Security" rising to 7th. This demonstrates that the successive implementation of the Hong Kong National Security Law, the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance and other relevant laws safeguarding national security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) has provided better protection for the security of the city and maintained it as an excellent environment for business and investment. Hong Kong has long been renowned as one of the safest cities in the world and consistently ranked as one of the least corrupt places in the world. Hong Kong has achieved remarkable results in fighting against graft and promoting integrity, as well as preventing and combating crimes. All these have injected strong stability to Hong Kong, fully demonstrating that security is a clear advantage for Hong Kong's development. In respect of "Constraints on Government Powers" and "Civil Justice", Hong Kong's rankings are same as last year. Hong Kong's rankings in the aspects of "Open Government" and "Regulatory Enforcement" remain almost unchanged, while its rankings slightly drop in the aspects of "Fundamental Rights" and "Criminal Justice". Under the protection of the "one country, two systems" principle and the Basic Law, Hong Kong has a robust legal framework for the protection of human rights and an open judicial system. The civil and criminal legal frameworks in Hong Kong align with international standards and keep up with the times, fully safeguarding the rights of the concerned parties. The Judiciary exercises judicial power independently in accordance with the law and is free from any interference. Under the Basic Law and the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance, parties may initiate legal proceedings and seek judicial remedies in accordance with the law, and are protected by a solid legal aid system. The HKSAR Government will continue to steadfastly safeguard the rights and freedoms enjoyed by Hong Kong residents under the law, and enhance its publicity and explanatory work through various channels to tell the good story of Hong Kong's rule of law to the international community. A robust rule of law is the cornerstone of Hong Kong's continuous high-quality development under the "one country, two systems" principle and a core advantage that underpins its position as an international legal hub. As the only bilingual common law jurisdiction in the world using Chinese and English, Hong Kong will give full play to its unique advantages to contribute to the upholding of the impartial and reasonable international rule of law and order, with its dispute-resolution rules and mechanisms aligned with international standards. The HKSAR Government will continue to comprehensively uphold the rule of law in the HKSAR, safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests under the rule of law, promote the rule of law education, and contribute to the cultivation of foreign-related legal talent.
